source.title: Language Models "Grok" to Copy
source.authors: Ang Lv; Ruo-Bing Xie; Xing-Wu Sun; Zhan-Hui Kang; Rui Yan

record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed copying development during pretraining of small Llama models on RedPajama text, a new setting relative to grokking on small algorithmic datasets.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own copying, loss, ICL-score, induction-head, and regularization results. Results about grokking cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains 162M Llama models on RedPajama text. It reports that context-copying accuracy surges long after pretraining loss stabilizes, a grokking-like delay in a new, realistic language-model pretraining setting. Its own results bear on V4 and on the non-algorithmic-data part of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue copying develops like grokking on three grounds: a sudden copying rise long after loss stabilizes; onset set by update steps, independent of token count; and induction heads forming shallow to deep. They report that regularization (dropout, weight decay) accelerates or improves copying, and note that copying is simpler than ICL, which they did not evaluate.
record.recipe_differences: The study pretrains small Llama models on RedPajama text and evaluates copying of random token subsequences; it does not use the small algorithmic-dataset training and test procedure of the original grokking study.
record.method_sensitivity: Copying development varies with batch size and learning rate; dropout advances the reported rise and increases fluctuations.

fits_no_version.finding: 10% attention dropout advances the copying jump from 15B to 10B tokens, with more fluctuation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-norm regularizers such as dropout accelerate grokking-like delayed capability onset in LM pretraining.

fits_no_version.finding: The onset of grokked copying is set by update steps and learning rate, not by token count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like onset in pretraining depends on optimization intensity (steps × learning rate) rather than data quantity.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The models are small and the copying task is a limited proxy for in-context ability; the paper says it could not evaluate robust ICL. Several results are conveyed qualitatively from figures without exact values or error bars. The induction-head evolution result is from a single model.

untested.parts: No small algorithmic datasets and no train/test accuracy; no dependence of the delay on training-set size.
No test of whether circuit measures anticipate the jump, and no measurement of memorizing-component removal.
No manipulation of initialization scale or weight norm, and no lazy-to-rich transition.
No fine-tuning, no models beyond 162M, and no task other than synthetic copying.
No efficiency comparison of circuits, no critical dataset size, and no ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.
No test of optimizer or numerical artifacts.

missing.what: Figure 4: training-loss convergence is token-count dependent while copying varies with update steps across batch sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The analogy is loose: single-pass pretraining has no overfitting, and 'fit' is loss stabilization. Results are figure-only, without error bars. The induction-head result comes from one model. The stated default learning rate (0.1) conflicts with the Figure 5 learning rates. The model is small (162M), so V4 support covers small-scale pretraining only.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train on small algorithmic datasets or report training and test accuracy in that setting.

It measures induction-head development during copying pretraining, but does not test whether memorizing components are removed or whether continuous circuit measures anticipate the accuracy jump in the stated algorithmic-task setting.
It reports delayed copying on text pretraining data, but does not test initialization scale, weight-norm manipulation, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
It tests small-model pretraining and a copying task only; it does not test fine-tuning, large models, or delayed generalization on broader realistic tasks.
It tests dropout and weight decay effects on copying, but not whether regularization selects a more efficient circuit over memorization, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The study does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause the delay.

conditions.value: 40 billion tokens from a subset of RedPajama

rows.measure: Context-copying test accuracy over training tokens
rows.value: Figure only; the text says accuracy remains low until 10B tokens and surges at 15B tokens.
rows.note: The text describes a clear delayed increase; the reported curve averages across three random seeds.
rows.check: The link is fine. Caveat: this is single-pass pretraining, so the 'training fit' is loss stabilization, not memorization or overfitting of a small train set. The delay is relative to loss, not to train accuracy.

rows.subject: small Llama model
rows.operation_detail: Track induction-head scores across layers during training
rows.value: Figure only; text says induction heads develop from shallower to deeper layers during training.
rows.note: The paper defines the score as a measure of induction-head strength and describes its layerwise development.
rows.check: Induction scores are shown developing shallow-to-deep in a single model. The text does not relate their timing to the copying-accuracy jump, nor say whether they rise gradually before it. Memorizing-component removal is not measured. So the row cannot show whether progress measures anticipate the jump.

rows.subject: small Llama model
rows.operation_detail: Track the ICL score and compare its stabilization with copying-test improvement
rows.value: The score stabilizes at -0.5 nats; the text says test accuracy continues to improve after this point.
rows.note: The authors use this measure to argue that copying on training data has saturated while test copying continues to improve.
rows.check: The ICL score on training data stabilizes at about 1.85B tokens while test copying keeps improving. This is an additional delay indicator; the timing appears only in the Discussion text.

rows.subject: small Llama model
rows.baseline: Vanilla model; abrupt increase at 15B tokens
rows.value: Figure only; text says dropout advances the abrupt accuracy increase from 15B tokens to 10B tokens, with increased fluctuation.
rows.note: The paper says dropout accelerates copying acquisition.
rows.check: 10% attention dropout is not a low-norm bias, so the row does not measure what V5 names. It shows regularization advancing the copying jump from 15B to 10B tokens. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: small Llama model
rows.value: Figure only; the text says weight decay improves accuracy compared with the vanilla model.
rows.note: The text does not give the final accuracy values.
rows.check: Weight decay (λ=0.1) improves final copying accuracy (figure only). The text reports no timing change and no circuit-efficiency, critical-size or ungrokking result. It is also unclear whether the 'vanilla' AdamW run had zero weight decay.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5. Weight decay λ=0.1 improves final copying accuracy relative to vanilla; competing-circuit efficiency, memorization replacement, critical dataset size and ungrokking are not measured.
source_check.problem: Improved copying accuracy alone cannot establish even a partial instance of V5's circuit-efficiency mechanism.

source_check.notes:
Section 2 states learning rate 0.1, whereas Figure 5 labels rates 1e-4, 2e-4 and 4e-4; the default is unresolved. r2 is a reference trajectory for r1, not independent evidence.
The evidence concerns synthetic copying after natural-text pretraining; robust ICL tasks were not evaluated.
